summary: Describes a way to broadcast IP data one-way using the vertical blanking interval of television signals, the hidden gap between video frames. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: TV pictures have a tiny invisible pause between frames. This hides computer data in that pause so a TV signal can carry it too.

subtitle: How to broadcast IP datagrams one-way inside the hidden lines of a television picture.

tldr.problem: The same news, stock quotes and weather data were being sent over and over to individual clients, while broadcast networks had no standard way to carry IP data to many receivers at once.
tldr.mechanism: IP datagrams are framed SLIP-style, optionally with compressed UDP/IP headers, protected by forward error correction, and carried in 36-byte NABTS packets on the vertical blanking interval lines of a television signal.
tldr.outcome: It defines a one-way, point-to-multipoint IP service over television signals, with no return channel. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 2728 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1999, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself describes only a one-way service with no return channel.

sections.title: Broadcasting IP in the Blanking Interval
sections.content:
RFC 2728 describes a method for broadcasting IP data in one direction using the vertical blanking interval (VBI) of a television signal. The VBI is the non-viewable part of the signal. It can provide point-to-multipoint IP data services that relieve congestion in the traditional Internet access networks.

The motivation is stated plainly. Content such as news feeds, stock quotes, newsgroups and weather reports is typically sent repeatedly to individual clients rather than broadcast to the many users who want it. The RFC says a lack of standards, and the expense of hardware, had kept broadcast networks from delivering data to the home and office.

No return channel is described, and the RFC says none is possible in the VBI. Wherever possible the design reuses existing standards.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing the same newspaper to every house one at a time, you shout the news once and everybody with a radio hears it. This RFC does that for computer data using TV signals.

sections.title: The Protocol Stack
sections.content:
The design is a stack of layers, each with no knowledge of the data it carries. From the bottom up: a television signal (NTSC or similar) carries NABTS packets, which contain a forward error correction (FEC) scheme. The resulting serial data stream is split into frames by a SLIP-style framing protocol, the frames hold IP packets with optionally compressed headers, and UDP carries the application data.

NABTS is the North American Basic Teletext Standard, defined in EIA-516. It is traditionally used on 525-line systems such as NTSC. Another byte structure, WST, is traditionally used on 625-line systems such as PAL and SECAM, but the RFC notes there are exceptions and countries should be treated individually. This document specifies the NABTS byte structure.
sections.eli5: Think of a stack of boxes: the TV signal is the bottom box, and each box above it wraps the next one up, until the top box holds the actual message.

sections.title: Where the Data Rides: VBI Lines
sections.content:
A 525-line television frame has two fields of 262.5 scan lines. The first 21 lines of each field are not part of the picture and make up the VBI. The first 9 of those are used while the cathode ray returns to the top of the screen, which leaves 12 possible lines for data, broadcast 60 times a second. In some countries line 21 is reserved for closed captioning, leaving 11.

A 625-line frame has two fields of 312.5 lines. Lines 6 to 22 in the first field and 319 to 335 in the second are available, giving 17 possible lines broadcast 50 times a second.

Some of these lines are already used for proprietary data and testing services, so IP delivery becomes one more data service using some or all of the lines.
sections.eli5: The TV has a few lines at the top that nobody sees. Some are busy getting the picture ready, and the rest are free for sending data.

sections.title: The NABTS Packet
sections.content:
A NABTS packet is a 36-byte structure encoded onto one scan line. It starts with a two-byte clock synchronization and a one-byte byte synchronization field, which set the decoder's sampling rate and byte timing. Next come a three-byte Packet Address, a one-byte Continuity Index and a one-byte Packet Structure field, followed by a 26-byte data block.

The Packet Address is Hamming encoded with 4 data bits per byte, so there are 4096 possible addresses. They distinguish unrelated services that share a channel. The Continuity Index counts from 0 to 15 and goes up by one for each packet of a given address, so the decoder can notice lost packets.

Packet Structure values are D0 (data, no filler), 8C (data with filler) and A1 (FEC packet). Filler in the data block is marked by 0x15 followed by as many 0xEA bytes as needed. Data is byte-ordered least significant bit first.
sections.eli5: Each TV line carries one small envelope with an address, a counting number so the receiver can tell if one went missing, and room for a little data.

sections.title: Forward Error Correction
sections.content:
Because the channel is one-way, the receiver cannot ask for a resend, so FEC is needed. The scheme splits the serial stream into 364-byte bundles of 14 packets of 26 bytes. A function over each packet's 26 bytes produces two suffix bytes, completing the NABTS packet (8 + 26 + 2).

Two further packets carrying only FEC data, 28 bytes each, are appended to every 14. The first packet in a bundle has Continuity Index 0 and the two FEC packets have 14 and 15. Together the bundle forms a table of 16 rows and 28 columns, protected both horizontally and vertically.

Appendix A defines the mathematics (a Galois field, GF(2^8)). The scheme can correct single-bit errors, most double-bit errors, single-byte errors, and one or two missing packets in a bundle. The RFC says how well errors are corrected depends on the receiver's implementation.
sections.eli5: Since the receiver cannot ask the sender to repeat itself, extra clues are sent along with the data. If a few pieces get smudged or lost, the clues let the receiver work out what they were.

sections.title: Framing and Header Compression
sections.content:
IP packets are framed by a protocol identical to SLIP (RFC 1055), using the special characters END (0xc0) and ESC (0xdb). A data byte equal to END is sent as ESC followed by 0xdc, and a data byte equal to ESC is sent as ESC followed by 0xdd. Every framed packet begins with a schema byte; if its top bit is set, the field becomes two bytes, allowing 32768 additional schemas. Only schema 0x00 is defined, and all receivers must support it.

Schema 0x00 starts with a one-byte Compression Key: one bit says whether the header is compressed and seven bits give the group. With the bit at zero, the full 20-byte IP header and 8-byte UDP header are sent, and the receiver stores them for that group. With the bit at one, only the IP identification and UDP checksum fields are sent, and the receiver rebuilds the rest from the stored header. This is related to the TCP/IP header compression of RFC 1144, but differs because transmission is one-way.

Group values can be recycled after 60 seconds of nonuse, and receivers disregard compressed packets arriving 60 or more seconds after the last uncompressed packet of that group. Fragmented datagrams must use uncompressed headers. Every packet ends with a 32-bit CRC using the MPEG-2 transport stream algorithm (not the Ethernet one). The MTU is 1500 octets.
sections.eli5: If you keep sending letters to the same address, you can write the full address once and then just write a short code. The receiver remembers the full address, but forgets it after a minute, so it gets rewritten now and then.

sections.title: Addressing, IANA and Security
sections.content:
NABTS packet addressing is not regulated or standardized, so care is needed so that unrelated services on the same channel do not use the same packet address. The RFC notes that the marketplace has traditionally made amicable arrangements for distributing these addresses per channel. IP source addresses should let receivers tell sources apart when hosts share an insertion point.

IANA registers new schemas on a First Come First Served basis. Anyone can register one by providing a point of contact and a brief description, and publishing a full specification is encouraged but not required.

On security, the RFC says that as with any broadcast network, the data is accessible to anyone who can receive it. It assumes securing data is the job of other layers such as IPsec, TLS and suitable application-layer protocols.
sections.eli5: Anyone with a receiver can hear a broadcast, so secrets need to be locked up before they are sent. The mailbox numbers also have to be handed out so two senders do not use the same one.
